text: Leather as received from the tanner is not fit for harness; the currier supplies suppleness and durability by adding oil and grease, so preserving these materials is necessary to prevent premature decay.
Moisture is the great destroyer of harness: it absorbs the grease, hardens the fibre and makes the leather weak and brittle, and it rusts the metal of the mountings.
Only grease resists the effects of moisture on leather.

It is a mistake for a manufacturer to think that a customer's ignorance of harness care benefits him; the most successful maker is the one who produces the most durable article and teaches the buyer how to treat it.
Three months' exposure in a wareroom injures a harness as much as three months of constant use by a user who knows how to take care of it.
Leather strapping, if displayed at all, should be in glass cases impervious to dust and air, though no showcase can be made tight enough to fully exclude them.
The white mould often seen on leather is caused by grease being drawn to the surface by moisture.
Once leather is covered with white mould, the grease keeps being absorbed in all kinds of weather until the mould is removed.
To remove white mould from harness in stock: brush it off, rub with a dry cloth, then with a greasy rag or "shammy", and restore the polish with an old silk handkerchief.
Tarnished mountings on harness in stock are cleaned with a "shammy"; if that fails, remove them and clean with a little rotten stone.
Gilt mountings should not be exposed in the wareroom; when sample sets cannot be had, the gilt should be protected by wrapping it in tissue paper.
The parts of a harness should be hung on forms instead of pegs or hooks, except traces and reins, which should always be hung out straight.
"Daub" is a grease made of one part of neat's-foot oil and two parts of tallow: the tallow is thoroughly melted, the oil poured in, and the whole stirred until cold.
Harness made up for stock should not be gummed and hung in cases; all the plain leather should be covered with a thin coat of daub, which feeds the leather and prevents injury.
In stock, patent and fancy leather should be wrapped in soft paper, and every piece laid out straight and smooth in shallow drawers and covered with thick paper.
Russet strapping should be kept in dark cases or drawers, because sunlight is sure to affect the color, the most exposed parts changing the most.

Makers who fill orders at short notice make up traces, reins, turnbacks, docks, back-bands and other straight strapping in advance and lay them away in grease; when an order comes they only make the other parts, finish the straight straps and attach the mountings.
Keeping straight strapping made up in grease lets a maker keep his workmen employed at all times and avoid hiring extra hands in the busy season.
The harness room should be as far from the horses as the building allows, because the gases arising from the stable are very injurious to leather and mountings.
A harness room should have forms for bridles, pads, saddles and breechings, and hooks for reins, hames and traces; if there is no separate room, closets should be provided.

Harness wet by rain should be hung where it can dry, then rubbed well with a "shammy" or wash-leather before going into the storeroom, after which a little crown soap is applied and rubbed with the hands until the polish is restored.
Harness wet by sweat must be dried as quickly as possible, because the saline nature of perspiration rapidly absorbs the grease and hardens the leather.
During at least the first year, crown soap is all the oiling a coach or carriage harness needs, but team and other heavy harness require a stronger grease.
Harness in daily use should be cleaned and oiled as often as once a month.

To clean soft leather in the stable: wash it with water applied with a "shammy", wring the shammy nearly dry and rub the leather thoroughly, then apply a good harness oil; afterwards remove surplus grease with a rag and rub with old silk until the polish returns.

To treat hard, dry leather in the stable: wash and wet the straps enough to open the pores, lay them straight, apply neat's-foot oil when surface dry, then warm tallow with a brush; when the moisture has dried out, remove the surplus tallow, brush the stitching clean and apply harness black.
Mountings do not need to be scoured; gold should never be rubbed with anything harsher than the nap side of canton flannel.
Electro silver plate must be cleaned carefully because the plate is soft and the thin coating is easily removed; close plate silver will bear more scouring.
Close plate silver seldom needs more than rubbing with a "shammy" darkened with tripoli and lampblack; if very tarnished, the mountings are removed, washed in water and rubbed with tripoli.
Brass is the most difficult metal on a harness to keep clean, but rubbing it each day greatly reduces the labor.
